column2: The Wisconsin Division of Highways and Milwaukee County propose to build the 'Airport Spur,' a 1.5-mile, four-lane divided freeway on new alignment connecting Interstate 94 to General Mitchell Field airport on Milwaukee's south side, at an estimated cost of about $12-14 million. The project would run through south-side Milwaukee neighborhoods in transition from farmland to housing and light industry, displacing 9-11 families and 2-5 businesses and passing about 250 feet from Hamlin Garland Elementary School. Five build corridors plus 'do-nothing,' 'no-build,' and mass-transit alternatives were studied, with Corridor #5 selected as least disruptive; citizens also proposed alternatives such as upgrading College Avenue, building exclusive bus lanes on existing freeways, and a 750-foot tunnel section (rejected as not economically justifiable). Predicted 1990 noise at Hamlin Garland School and about 40 adjacent homes would exceed federal standards without mitigation, prompting proposed noise barriers, earth berms, and air conditioning of the school; the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources approved the project's air-quality analysis under the state Indirect Source Rules, finding carbon-monoxide levels would not exceed 75% of national standards. Public response was mixed: elected officials and citizens raised strong opposition on noise, air-quality, and school-impact grounds, while regional planning bodies and aviation groups supported it, and a November 1974 countywide advisory referendum approved the Spur 57.8% to 42.2%.

column2: The Wisconsin Division of Highways and Milwaukee County propose to build the 'Airport Spur,' a 1.5-mile, four-lane divided freeway on new alignment within Corridor #5, connecting Interstate 94 to General Mitchell Field airport on Milwaukee's south side. The project also widens I-94 from Layton Avenue to the spur connection by adding 13-foot lanes and a concrete median barrier, and includes an interchange at Howell Avenue. Right-of-way would be 300-350 feet wide, and the estimated total cost is about $12-14 million, with Milwaukee County paying $2.2 million and federal and state funds covering the rest. Projected 1990 traffic is roughly 19,600 vehicles per day, about 9% trucks.

column2: The EIS evaluated five build alternatives plus a 'do-nothing' option (make no changes) and a 'no-build' option (only improve local streets and arterials): upgrading Grange Avenue between Howell Avenue and I-94 into a multi-lane arterial; rapid transit service to the airport; and four freeway corridors on new alignment (Nos. 2, 3, 4, and the recommended No. 5, which is a revision of Corridor 3 shifted north to fit the new air-cargo area). Corridor #5 was selected as least disruptive; rejected build corridors had larger drawbacks — Corridor No. 4 alone would displace 230 people from 62 housing units. Rail rapid transit was rejected in favor of rubber-tired 'modified rapid transit' buses using the freeway, and forecast traffic was judged too low to justify an exclusive bus lane or shuttle. Citizens proposed additional alternatives — upgrading College Avenue instead of building the Spur, converting highway funds to exclusive bus lanes on the existing expressway system under Wis. Stat. Ch. 84.01(27), terminating the freeway at the Milwaukee Road rail line and using an at-grade parkway with a shuttle like O'Hare's, a 750-foot tunnel section from I-94 to 14th Street (about $5 million extra), and routing via the old North Shore railroad right-of-way from Rawson Avenue — which the Division addressed but rejected as not economically justifiable or not conforming to the regional plan.

column2: The largest human impact is land acquisition and displacement — about 35 acres removed from the local tax base (roughly $2.5 million), with 9-11 families and 2-5 businesses displaced. Predicted 1990 noise near the Spur, at Hamlin Garland School (site 15), and near the Howell Avenue interchange (site 24) would exceed the federal 70 dBA exterior / 55 dBA interior standards, and about 40 residents adjacent to the Spur would face noise above federal standards without mitigation; the Division proposes $350,000 in noise barriers plus earth berms and air-conditioning the school (dropping interior noise to 45 dBA). The entire corridor already lies within Mitchell Field's 100 Composite Noise Rating contour for aircraft. Critics faulted the air-quality analysis for using tons/day rather than parts-per-million, California-based emission factors, and omitting Lake Michigan 'lake effect' meteorology, but the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources — acting as the state's Indirect Source Review Agency under Wisconsin Administrative Code NR 154 — reviewed a worst-case microscale carbon-monoxide analysis and approved the project on November 20, 1975, finding no receptor would exceed 75% of national standards. DNR indicated no significant impact on fish, wildlife, or endangered species; no natural waterways would be crossed; and the State Historical Society found no known archaeological or historic sites would be affected.

column2: Public review included a Location Public Hearing on March 25, 1969 (about 120 attendees) and an Environmental Public Hearing on July 11, 1974 (about 150 attendees, 32 witnesses testifying). Regional and aviation interests — SEWRPC, FAA, AAA, the Milwaukee Air Cargo Association, and the Mitchell Field Director — supported the project, while State Senator Kurt Frank, State Representative John Plewa, private citizens including Robert Szyba ('Citizen's Against Airport Spur'), Wisconsin's Environmental Decade, and the Southeastern Wisconsin Coalition for Clean Air opposed it, chiefly over noise and air-quality effects on Hamlin Garland School and the surrounding neighborhood. The Milwaukee Common Council passed a May 2, 1973 resolution supporting removal of the Spur from the county expressway system, then on October 23, 1973 modified it to oppose construction until the project could handle truck traffic without being environmentally detrimental; the Wisconsin Highway Commission suspended right-of-way acquisition on March 12, 1973 pending the Final EIS. EPA Region V rated the Draft EIS 'LO-1' (no objection). In a countywide advisory referendum on November 5, 1974, voters approved building the Airport Spur 57.8% to 42.2%.
